pending.topic: Decoy effect: how a third pricing plan makes the middle one sell

post.hook: Why does a third plan push sales?
slides: When you offer only two plans – $19 basic and $49 premium – many prospects stare at the price gap. Adding a $39 “standard” plan, which looks only slightly cheaper than premium, nudges them toward the $49 option.
Psychologists call this the **decoy effect**. The extra middle tier is deliberately unattractive, yet it changes how we compare the other two.
Our brain evaluates options **relatively**, not absolutely. The decoy creates a reference point that makes the higher-priced plan appear more valuable for only a little extra cost.
Marketers exploit this by positioning the decoy **close in price** to the premium but with fewer features, so the premium seems like the best bang-for-buck.
A classic experiment by Ariely (2008) showed that 70 % of participants chose the premium when a decoy was present, versus 30 % without it.
In practice, SaaS companies often list three tiers: **Starter $19**, **Growth $39**, **Pro $49**. The Growth plan is the decoy that drives upgrades to Pro.
When designing your pricing page, add a decoy that is **just a shade cheaper** than your target plan, but with noticeably fewer benefits.
post.takeaway: Add a strategically placed middle tier that’s only marginally cheaper than your premium offering, and watch the premium’s conversion rate climb. Test the three-tier layout against a two-tier version to confirm the lift.
post.caption:
Ever wondered why a third pricing option can make the middle one look bland and the top one irresistible? It’s not magic – it’s the decoy effect at work.

By giving prospects a reference point that feels like a compromise, you subtly steer them toward the option that delivers the most profit. A well-placed decoy can boost your premium conversions by double-digits.
